TL;DR: It is very easy to grow, but takes a while to germinate.

Sometime in April (zone 9b) I simply filled a 7-gallon bucket with a mixture of compost, vermiculite and peat-moss. Watered it thoroughtly and let it drain. Made a small depression in the middle and put a whole chayote in it. Covered the top with a loose lid to keep out pests, set the bucket in full sun.

After about 3 to 4 weeks of absolutely no progress, I gave up and repurposed the container to grow carrots. I left the chayote in it, because I figured it would just decompose. Got my harvest of carrots in a few weeks, still no sign of life in the chayote.

I then had a couple of tomato suckers I had pruned, and randomly stuck those in the pot (at this point this was pretty much an experimental container). The tomatoes grew into plants and are now producing fruit. I had forgotten about the chayote at this point.

Just a couple of weeks ago, I was pruning back the tomatoes and noticed a chayote vine growing in the middle. It had been over 3 months since I put it in the container.

Once they get going, they are vigorous and aggressive growers and will sprawl or climb wherever you let them. You have to keep cutting back the growing tips pretty much every 3 days. You can also expect to get a generous yield, as long as you maintain a good watering schedule. My friend has a vine growing in her backyard, overwintered in zone 9b and it is prolific. I have not yet seen a flower set in my vine yet, perhaps because of nutrient competition with the tomatoes in the same container. Once the current bunch of tomatoes ripen, I plan to pull and toss out the tomatoes, and give this a dose of fertilizer to see if I can get the chayote to get productive.
